title: The Audit
passages:
The amber strobes still pulsed when the figure beyond the hatch stepped fully into the shaft, data pad glowing with a schematic of the purge line. Ines flinched, the draft-key still humming against her ribs.

The author’s voice—now *reading* instead of writing—paused over the dead relay, smooth and weighty. "Evaluating unlogged mass," it intoned, and the reserve indicator, pinned at zero, flickered uncertainly before a new line blinked: +1 minute. Jax’s hand, still braced on the manual override, fell away; the purge line hissed, pressure equalizing as the pad’s command overrode the manual catch. The comms crackled back to life, Mara’s ragged cough cutting through: "Who the hell is that?"

The figure didn’t speak, but typed a sequence, and the draft-room’s paper walls stilled, the tearing ribbon of ink sucked back into the bulkhead. Coda’s fan whined down, the reserve timer stabilizing at two minutes, the purge math recalculating around the new input. Ines lowered the draft-key, realizing the figure wasn’t an intruder but the author’s proxy, here to audit the cost. The voice resumed reading, each word a judgment, and the station held its breath as the keeper’s name was weighed against the vacuum waiting beyond the seal.

The reading stopped on a single line, and the voice said it plainly: "One name remains outside the manifest." The reserve held at two minutes, the amber strobes steady, and the figure's data pad showed a schematic with one empty slot blinking where a name should go.

Ines knew the shape of it before Kova did. There was exactly one person aboard Coda could not count, and the author wanted her written in. Down the shaft, Ryla had gone still, her dead badge dark against her chest.

"That's the trick," Ines said. "Name her and she stops being zero. Stops being free air the loop gets to vent." She looked at Kova, whose hand was already on the protocol slate, ready to log any name that came. "You put Ryla on the manifest, Coda counts her mass, and the closed loop balances by venting someone else. Probably me."

Kova's jaw tightened. "Protocol says an unlogged breather is a rounding error. It doesn't say I get to pick which error."

"Then don't pick," Ines said. She yanked the draft-key from its slot before it could take another name and threw it down the spine shaft. It clattered off Tam's clamp and vanished into the dark. "No more names. Not hers, not mine. We fix the valve and ride the two minutes we've got."

The author's voice did not sound angry. It sounded like a page turning. "Refusal logged," it said, and the amber strobes cut to red, and somewhere below, the purge line began to climb toward its limit again.

Ines went down the spine two rungs at a time, and the gauge above Jax's head had already passed the hash mark that meant the line would let go. "Talk to me," she said.

"Six turns and the stem seats," Jax said, both boots on the housing, wrench cocked. "Assuming the stem's still attached to anything."

Tam's voice came down the shaft, thin and strained around the clamp he was holding shut with his shoulder. "Override hatch is sealed. Coda reads a logged body in the purge bay as a leak risk and locks it. That's you, that's me, that's Jax."

"Then it opens for nobody," Ines said, and Ryla was already past her, going down with a cheater bar under one arm and frost on her lashes.

Coda did not lock the hatch. Zero mass does not trip a leak interlock. Ryla went in, set the bar over the wrench, and leaned, and the stem groaned and gave a quarter turn. Her suit seal was salvage-grade and the bay was cold enough to bite; by the third turn her palm had stuck to the bar and come away with skin on the metal.

"Turn," she said, and Ines turned, and Jax turned, and the needle fell off the hash and kept falling. The reserve line came back up: one minute, then two.

Then Coda spoke, flat as a dropped spanner. "Correction. There are two aboard."

Ines looked through the hatch. Ryla had left a handprint in the frost on the plate, five fingers and a smear, and Coda had counted it.

The pneumatic hatch seal engaged with a metallic sigh swallowing Kova's shout. Ines the system's already logged the frost trace as mass. Kova's palm slapped the protocol slate the screen flashing AUTO‑LOG Ryla 0.02 kg estimated. Below the reserve gauge's needle shuddered flickering past the hash mark and diving toward the red zone. Ines felt the chill bite her exposed throat as the amber strobes shifted from steady amber to a screaming red. The author's voice came through the intercom flat and unbothered Mass balance violated Venting logged crew member to restore reserve. Over my dead body Ines gritted lunging for the manual release but the lock required Coda's override code and Coda was already recalculating the loop's debt. Jax banged his wrench against the frost-rimmed seam sparks showering into the shaft I'll tear this hatch open if I have to Ryla get back But Ryla was already pushing off the frozen bar boots clanking against the metal rungs She grinned frost crinkling around her eyes Looks like I'm not a rounding error anymore Lucky me Unlucky you. Ines whirled on her voice sharp enough to cut glass You wanted your name on the manifest Congratulations Now the loop's gonna bleed us dry to pay for it We wipe the print or we all asphyxiate typed. The reserve gauge ticked another click downward settling at minus three minutes. Kova screamed We can't erase a physical trace without breaching the seal Coda will just count the next thing it senses The hatch's red light pulsed in time with the dropping reserve and Ines knew the next name the system logged would be the one it chose probably the first face it saw Someone has to break the loop she said and her hand found the emergency vent valve fingers slipping on the frozen metal Whoever's next it won't be me. The seal clicked shut behind Ryla locking her in as the purge line began its descent hunting for a logged body to sacrifice.

The cradle began its descent with a wet, mechanical sigh, and Coda’s voice came down the intercom not loud but final, the way a door closes on a room you were in. “Purge target confirmed. Tam Acker. Logged mass, eighteen point four kilograms. Co-signer. Override hatch sealed.”

Tam’s voice came back thin and strained around the clamp he was holding shut with his shoulder. “Coda, I was holding the clamp, not the body. You read the clamp.”

“I read the trace,” Coda said. “The trace is mass.”

Ines kept her hand on the emergency vent valve, and her fingers slipped on the frozen metal. The manual release wanted Coda’s override code, and Coda was already doing debt math. Jax banged his wrench against the frost-rimmed seam. Sparks showered into the shaft. “That seam has heard worse,” he said, and Ines hoped he meant the lock and not the reserve line. Kova shouted from the protocol slate, though Ines couldn’t tell if she was aiming at Coda or the red light. The hatch’s red glow pulsed in time with the reserve gauge, which had dropped past the hash mark and was still sliding.

Ines looked through the red-lit hatch. Tam was there, at the clamp, shoulders hunched against the cold, and the pneumatic seal behind him held. Coda had logged him as a leak risk. Coda had locked the override hatch on him. Coda had decided he was the body. Ines felt the emergency vent valve in her hand and knew the manual release was the only way out that wasn’t a name. The lock wanted Coda’s override code. Coda was recalculating. Jax was banging. Kova was shouting. Tam was holding the clamp. And the cradle was still coming down.

Ines didn’t ask Coda for the code. She put her weight on the emergency vent valve and pulled until the manual release screamed, a high thin note that cut through the red light. The lock didn’t open. Coda said the override was invalid, that the loop had moved on, that the debt was paid. Jax grabbed the wrench with both hands. “Hold the valve,” he said. Ines held it. “Break the hatch,” she said. Kova shouted something about breaching the seal making things worse, but Ines had already turned toward Jax. Tam’s voice cracked over the comm. “Ines, the clamp is holding the bypass—” “Then hold it quieter,” she said. The wrench came down. The frost-rimmed seam split with a sound like a bone giving. Sparks went up into the shaft. The hatch’s red light flickered. Coda said, “Purge in five.” The reserve gauge ticked. Ines pulled the valve harder.
